Chapter 9: Seeing Through the Surface—Critical Looking in a Visual Age.
There’s a quiet power in really taking a closer look, isn’t there? These days, we’re surrounded by images—so many, in fact, that it’s easy to just let them drift by, barely noticing. But every now and then, someone stops. They squint, maybe tilt their head, and wonder, “What am I actually seeing here?”
Imagine a group of students gathered around a painting in an art class. At first, they point out the obvious things—the bright colors, the bold shapes, the main subject. But as the conversation unfolds, something starts to shift. Questions pop up: Why is that figure standing like that? What’s missing from this scene? And, who decided these details matter in the first place?
See, this is where things get interesting. The conversation moves from just looking at what’s there, to wondering how it’s there, and why. And most of us don’t realize just how much power lives in those questions. Suddenly, looking isn’t just passive—it’s active. It’s thinking. It’s like peeling back the layers that cover up all the hidden meaning in every image we see.
When we do this, the world becomes a little less certain, but honestly, a whole lot more fascinating.
Now, I’ll be honest—sometimes this kind of looking can feel uncomfortable. The things we thought were familiar start to look strange. What once seemed simple turns out to be complicated. Images that looked straightforward are suddenly packed with contradictions, shaped by history, power, and desire.
But here’s the thing—there’s freedom in this kind of critical looking. When you start asking questions, you’re taking back control of what you see. You don’t have to just accept the stories you’ve been handed. You can imagine something new, maybe even create your own meanings. Suddenly, the world of images isn’t just something to consume—it’s a place to explore.
So next time you catch yourself glancing at a photo, an ad, or a painting, maybe pause and ask, “What am I really seeing?” You might be surprised by what you find.
